concepts.name: Improve your worst-placed piece
concepts.wording: Find the piece doing least and improve it - or exchange it for one of the opponent's best. It works because a position's strength is the sum of what its pieces do, so the cheapest improvement available is to the piece contributing least.
cautions: Identifying the worst piece is a judgement, not a measurement. This system has no reliable detector for it and must not claim one.
Anderssen's own exception: when immediate advantage is available from an attack.

An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

It attacks weak pawns, escorts passed pawns and blockades enemy ones, and the side whose king arrives first usually wins endings that look level.
cautions: Rook endings, where the author of the principle records finding outright incorrect centralisation and attributes it to their concreteness and to the king's larger defensive role.
Positions where the king is still exposed to checks that gain the opponent tempi.

concepts.name: Passed pawn
concepts.wording: A passed pawn: no enemy pawn ahead of it on its file or either neighbour, so only pieces can stop it. Its worth depends almost entirely on whether it can advance — a permanently blockaded passer is a liability rather than an asset.
cautions: PROVEN EXCEPTION to Tarrasch's 'rook behind the passed pawn': in the Vancura configuration — a rook pawn on the sixth with the attacking rook in front of it — putting the rook behind the pawn LOSES. Tablebase-verified on a pair differing only in the defending rook's square: beside the pawn is a draw, behind it is a loss in 63. See `vancura-position`.
A blockaded passer that ties down its owner's pieces is a liability, not an asset. Nimzowitsch's blockade rule is right about half the time, which is the honest figure.

concept.name: Pawn promotion
concept.wording: Promotion: a pawn arriving on the eighth rank is replaced immediately, as part of the same move, by a piece of its own colour. The choice is free and unlimited — a side may have several queens — and it is not confined to pieces already captured.

Underpromotion to a rook avoids stalemate where a queen would cause it; underpromotion to a knight gains a check or fork unavailable to a queen.

concepts.name: Space advantage
concepts.wording: A space advantage: you control more squares behind your pawn front. The value is mobility — their pieces get in each other's way. Avoid exchanges, and find an entry square, because space without a way in wins nothing.
cautions: Space with no way in is worth little.
Space bought by overextension is a liability — the hypermodern critique.

concept.name: Exchange sacrifice
concept.wording: An exchange sacrifice: rook for a minor piece. First check whether it is forced — if mate or material follows by force, calculate it. If not, name the lasting asset it buys.
cautions: In open positions with files available, a rook is worth more than the nominal margin and the sacrifice is correspondingly worse.
Returning the exchange at the right moment is a standard resource for the defender and must be accounted for.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.wording: A sacrifice. First ask whether the material comes back by force: if it does, calculate it and stop worrying. If it does not, you are judging the compensation instead.
cautions: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

The blanket rule 'trade pieces against an IQP' has an important qualification: trade MINOR pieces, but keep a queen and a rook, or there is nothing left to attack the pawn with.

concept.name: Blockade
concept.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

concepts.name: Pawn break
concepts.wording: A pawn break: an advance into contact with an enemy pawn, played to open a file or a diagonal for the pieces behind it, or to force the opponent's structure to commit. It is not played to win a pawn.
cautions: A break that opens lines for a better-developed opponent helps them.
Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

concept.wording: A bad bishop — its own pawns sit on the squares it travels on, so its diagonals are blocked from the inside and the squares they leave uncovered are ones the bishop cannot use either. The cures are a pawn break, a trade, or getting the bishop outside the chain.

A bad bishop defending a colour complex is doing essential work and should not be traded off casually.

concept.name: Battery
concept.wording: A battery: two long-range pieces on the same file, rank or diagonal, with nothing of their own between them. The front piece can capture and the rear one recaptures, so the pair attacks with more force than either alone.
cautions: Ordering matters: queen in front of rook is usually worse than rook in front of queen, because the more valuable piece meets the defenders first.
Two line pieces on one line are only a battery if the line ARRIVES somewhere. Stacked behind their own pawns they combine nothing, and the bare geometry fires on nearly half of all positions.

altConcept.name: Weak square
altConcept.wording: e6 is a weak square — no friendly pawn can attack it, and pawns cannot move backwards, so it stays weak. That matters when an enemy piece can occupy it and cannot be driven off.
cautions: A weak square covered by a piece is not exploitable while that piece stays; the plan is to trade it off first.
Conceding weak squares is routinely the right price for space, the bishop pair, or a tempo.

cautions: Restraining an advance the opponent did not want is a wasted move.
In sharp positions speed beats restraint.

concepts.name: King safety
concepts.wording: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.
cautions: An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

concepts.wording: A trapped piece: every square it can reach loses it just the same, so attacking it wins it. Not a pin and not a fork — the piece is free to move and has nowhere to go.
cautions: A trapped piece may escape by a desperado capture, or by a counter-threat that gains the tempo it needs.

concepts.name: Hanging piece

concepts.wording: A piece that is attacked and can be captured for free — undefended, or defended fewer times than it is attacked.
cautions: A hanging piece may be a sacrifice offered on purpose. SEE says the material is winnable; it does not say taking is right.
In a lost position, giving material to reach a fortress or a perpetual can be correct.

concepts.name: Blockade
concepts.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

concepts.name: Check
concepts.wording: Check: the king is attacked, and the side to move has exactly three ways to answer — move the king, block the line, or capture the attacker. Nothing else is legal, which is why a check is the most forcing move there is.
cautions: A check being available is not a reason to play it. Proven case: Ra7+ draws and Rg8+ loses in the same position.
A pinned piece still delivers check — being unable to legally move does not stop a piece attacking the king.

concepts.name: Opposite-coloured bishops
concepts.wording: Opposite-coloured bishops: the bishops can never contest the same squares, so the defender can blockade on their own colour and the attacker's bishop can never challenge it. One extra pawn usually draws and two often do — on one wing. Passed pawns far enough apart beat a lone bishop, because it has to choose.
cautions: The drawish rule is an endgame rule. With queens and rooks on, opposite bishops favour the attacker.
Three files of separation between passed pawns usually wins despite the bishops.

concepts.name: Blockade
concepts.wording: Blockade: park a piece directly in front of an enemy pawn so it cannot advance. A knight is the ideal blockader because it keeps all its power from the square; a queen is the worst, because any minor piece evicts her.
cautions: A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.

cautions: Rook endings, where the author of the principle records finding outright incorrect centralisation and attributes it to their concreteness and to the king's larger defensive role.
Positions where the king is still exposed to checks that gain the opponent tempi.

concepts.name: Pawn break

Some positions are won by NOT breaking — keeping the tension is itself a plan, and the threat can be worth more than the move.

cautions: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

concepts.name: Control of the centre
concepts.wording: Control of the centre: influence over the four central squares, whether by occupying them with pawns or attacking them from a distance with pieces. Occupation gives space; control without commitment avoids giving a target.
cautions: Occupying the centre is not always right — an unsupported pawn centre is a target, which is the hypermodern case.
Ceding the centre is not always right either — against proper support it just loses space.

moves.text: Moving the pawn uncovers the queen on g7, which now checks the king. It comes with check, so the reply is not a free move. It wins the pawn. A discovered attack: two attacks for one move — whatever the moving piece does, and whatever the piece behind it now hits. The moving piece is comparatively free, because the opponent has to deal with the revealed threat.

concepts.name: Trapped piece
concepts.why: The knight on f3 is trapped — every square it can reach loses it.
concepts.wording: A trapped piece: every square it can reach loses it just the same, so attacking it wins it. Not a pin and not a fork — the piece is free to move and has nowhere to go.
cautions: A trapped piece may escape by a desperado capture, or by a counter-threat that gains the tempo it needs.

concepts.name: Discovered check
concepts.wording: A discovered check: the piece that moves is not the piece that checks, so the reply must answer the check and the moving piece is free to take, threaten or run wherever it likes. That freedom is the whole value of the motif.
cautions: If the discovered check can be met by a capture of the checking piece, the free move is not free.

A relative pin can be broken profitably when moving the front piece creates a bigger threat.

concepts.wording: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.

An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.

concept.name: En passant capture
concept.wording: En passant: when a pawn advances two squares and lands beside an enemy pawn, that pawn may capture it as if it had moved one square. The right lasts exactly one move and then disappears.
cautions: Cannot be deferred: the right is lost if not exercised immediately.
Like any move, it is illegal if it leaves or places one's own king in check.

concepts.name: Opposite-coloured bishops
concepts.wording: Opposite-coloured bishops: the bishops can never contest the same squares, so the defender can blockade on their own colour and the attacker's bishop can never challenge it. One extra pawn usually draws and two often do — on one wing. Passed pawns far enough apart beat a lone bishop, because it has to choose.
cautions: The drawish rule is an endgame rule. With queens and rooks on, opposite bishops favour the attacker.
Three files of separation between passed pawns usually wins despite the bishops.

concepts.wording: A sacrifice. First ask whether the material comes back by force: if it does, calculate it and stop worrying. If it does not, you are judging the compensation instead.
cautions: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.

concepts.name: King safety
concepts.wording: King safety: count the attackers that can reach the king's area against the defenders already there. One or two is normal; three against a damaged shield is when sacrifices start to work.
cautions: An exposed king is not a losing king. In a proven drawn ending both kings stand in the open with no pawn shelter, and centralising them is correct - see the recorded counterexample.
An exposed king with no attackers left is an ACTIVE king, and in the endgame that is what you want.
